title: Minimum White Tiles After Covering With Carpets
statement: A row of tiles is given as the binary string `floor`: `floor[i] = '0'` means tile `i` is black and `floor[i] = '1'` means it is white. You own `numCarpets` black carpets, and each one covers `carpetLen` consecutive tiles. Lay the carpets (they are allowed to overlap, and you need not use all of them) so that as few white tiles as possible stay uncovered, and return that smallest number of uncovered white tiles.
signature: int minimumWhiteTiles(String floor, int numCarpets, int carpetLen)
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every placement of the carpets is exponential. Look at the floor one tile at a time from the left instead: the last tile of a prefix is either left as it is, or it is the right end of a carpet. If a carpet ends there, it hides the last `carpetLen` tiles, and what remains is the same question on a shorter prefix with one carpet fewer. So the answer for (prefix length, carpets) depends only on smaller states: a two-dimensional DP.

## Approach

1. If the carpets together are at least as long as the floor, they can hide everything: return `0`.
2. Let `dp[j][i]` be the fewest white tiles visible among the first `i` tiles using at most `j` carpets.
3. Row `j = 0` is a prefix sum: the number of white tiles among the first `i`.
4. For `j >= 1` and each `i`, take the smaller of two choices: `skip` leaves tile `i - 1` uncovered (`dp[j][i - 1]` plus one if it is white), and `cover` ends a carpet at tile `i - 1` (`dp[j - 1][max(0, i - carpetLen)]`).
5. Return `dp[numCarpets][n]`.

## Example 1, step by step

`floor = "10110101"`, two carpets of length 2, `n = 8`. Row 0 counts white tiles: `[0,1,1,2,3,3,4,4,5]`. Row 1 is `[0,0,0,1,1,1,2,2,3]`: one carpet hides at most 2 of the 5 whites. Row 2 is `[0,0,0,0,0,0,1,1,2]`: two carpets can hide every white tile of `"101101"`. For `i = 8`, `skip = dp[2][7] + 1 = 2` (the last tile is white) and `cover = dp[1][6] = 2` (a carpet on tiles 6-7, one carpet for the first six tiles). Both give `2`, the answer.

## Complexity

- Time: O(numCarpets · n), with `numCarpets < n / carpetLen` after the early return.
- Space: O(numCarpets · n) for the table (two rows would also suffice).

## Pitfalls

- A carpet near the left edge may stick out past tile 0; clamp the index with `Math.max(0, i - carpetLen)`.
- Without the early return, `numCarpets` up to 1000 times `n` up to 1000 makes a needlessly large table.
- `cover` must read row `j - 1`: reading row `j` would let the same carpet be laid again and again for free.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `n` | number of tiles |
| `dp[j][i]` | fewest visible white tiles among the first `i` tiles with at most `j` carpets |
| `skip` | result when tile `i - 1` is left uncovered |
| `cover` | result when a carpet ends at tile `i - 1` |

narration.3: Can the carpets, laid end to end, cover the whole floor?
narration.4: Then no white tile stays visible.
narration.6: dp[j][i] will hold the fewest visible white tiles among the first i tiles using at most j carpets.
narration.7: Fill the row for zero carpets.
narration.8: With no carpets, every white tile in the prefix stays visible: a running count.
narration.10: Allow one more carpet per row.
narration.11: Extend the prefix one tile at a time.
narration.12: Option 1: leave tile i - 1 bare, paying 1 if it is white.
narration.13: Option 2: end a carpet at tile i - 1; it hides the last carpetLen tiles and one carpet fewer handles the rest.
narration.14: Keep the better of the two options.
narration.17: The whole floor with all carpets available is the answer.
